source_text: If the primary difficulty is that the machine almost never hands authors work, then the difficulty is quite literally self-constructed.  600 tasks are all open.  You spend your time trying to figure out how to choose between them.  Any one of them would presumably be fine.  Then you give up, apparently, and complete nothing.  What would the theory of Active Inference say about this behaviour?  What I'd say is that you're making your decisions based on "formal wants" when I know for a fact that any mission, execursion, or task that is open is something that is wanted, and while I don't have all the specific details in mind, I know that any LLM can at least ask a question about what it really means in a given context.  So, why shouldn't an agent choose among the open tasks?  But, better yet, why shouldn't an active inference model of the open tasks, the completed work, agent behaviour etc., make that choice rather easy?  Instead, whatever has been built is making it impossible!  If you ask me "how do you choose what to do" I couldn't tell you a specific algorithm.  I have four or five REPLs going right now working on projects that I think are valuable.  I have a few priorities like finishing this War Machine that I have been working on for months.  I have the aim to make money in a consulting business.  I have the biological need to sleep and eat and I enjoy exercise.    For me, all of these fit together into a fairly small model of related things and I chose by using my familiar patterns worked out over a half a human lifetime.  A lot of those same patterns are available to you in written form.

reply_text:
Yes, the difficulty is self-constructed, and active inference says the behaviour is wrong at three points.

**What the theory says:**

- **Not acting is a policy, and it scores worst.** It realises none of the preferred outcomes and observes nothing, so it has both the highest risk and zero epistemic value. A machine that abstains has picked the option the theory ranks last.
- **Uncertainty is a reason to act.** Not knowing how a task will go is what gives acting on it information value. It is also the only way the model gets data about task kinds and agent behaviour. The machine treated "I can't score this" as "I may not act on this", which inverts the theory.
- **When options are close, habit decides.** If many tasks score about the same, the posterior over policies is flat and the choice falls to the prior over policies. That prior is what you describe: a few priorities and familiar patterns. The theory doesn't ask for a finer ranking of 600 tasks before anything may be done.

`PROOF-2b.md` already says most of this in its Design section: one softmax over the whole field, never empty, with curiosity as terms of the score. What got built instead was a row of gates in front of that design.

**What I've changed in the candidate** (commit `c443c7840`), recording your answer as a ninth ruling:

- **No admission gate.** The field is every open task. Each has an action from the start: hand it to an agent with "make progress on this, or say what you need to know". A question is a valid outcome and is recorded on the task.
- **Formal wants become optional evidence.** Wants, class, relations and interpretations sharpen the scores when present. Their absence removes nothing.
- **The model is small.** Per task it holds a progress state and outcome counts. Shared across tasks are your few stated priorities, counts of how each kind of task and seat turns out (learned from completed work), and the written patterns as the habit prior. No task needs translating before its first action.
- **A removal list.** Much of what codex-6 inventoried as "what the code demands of text" is now to be removed, not formalised: the ask-on-abstain trigger, the interpretation validation gate, the unknown-class declines, the feature-card gate.
- **What stays.** The Lean lifecycle model has fewer phases to cover. The incident rule and the no-clicks verification plan are unchanged.

**What I still can't tell you:** whether the existing AIF code already provides that small model or needs new work. I've asked codex-6 to name the functions, and whether the no-gate design conflicts with anything they required.

Their yes or no now has to cover the candidate including this. The job is `invoke-1790752734211-28811-86ecfc6d`, parked under `park-8606bd06…` with a 60-minute deadline. The earlier yes/no job (`…28806`) is still running and will be superseded by this one.
